# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been uncomfortable, but climate change has transformed it from a seasonal nuisance into a genuine public health crisis. Heat now kills more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the toll falls disproportionately on city dwellers. This is not an accident of geography but a product of design. Cities concentrate heat: asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation all day and release it slowly at night, buildings block cooling breezes, vehicles and air conditioners pump out waste heat, and the scarcity of vegetation removes both shade and evaporative cooling. The result is the urban heat island effect, in which dense neighborhoods can run five to ten degrees Fahrenheit hotter than their leafier surroundings. The good news is that heat is one of the few climate hazards cities can meaningfully reduce through deliberate design choices. The challenge is that every intervention carries tradeoffs, and the residents who suffer most from heat are often the least equipped to navigate those tradeoffs.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

Street trees remain the single most effective tool for cooling urban neighborhoods. A mature canopy can reduce surface temperatures by twenty to forty degrees Fahrenheit compared to exposed pavement, and shade lowers the perceived temperature for pedestrians dramatically.
